newsitem.title: USA: Yield curve in US leading indicators sparks debate.
newsitem.headline: Yield curve in US leading indicators sparks debate.

text.p: Experts are debating whether a yield curve measure the Conference Board will add to its U.S. leading indicators will improve the index's ability to predicting turning points in the U.S. economy.

The Conference Board has eliminated the sensitive materials prices and order backlogs measures from what critics have called the "misleading indicators index." In the new index, to be released Monday, those measures will be replaced with the spread between yields of the federal funds rate and the 10-year U.S. Treasury note.

The new index "looks much smoother," said Delos Smith, senior business analyst at the Conference Board, which last year assumed the job of compiling the index formerly produced by the U.S. Commerce Department. "Hopefully, it will (predict) peaks and troughs in the economy better than before, and hopefully, it will not give as many false signals."

The leading indicator index has drawn ridicule in recent years from market players and economists for acting more like a coincident indicator. Economists wonder whether adding the yield spread between fed funds and the 10-year note will transform the index into a useful indicator.
Steven Wieting, associate economist at Smith Barney Inc, said the yield spread does indeed work as a leading indicator.

Since 1959, "The spread (between funds and the 10-year note) has fallen or was negative prior to a recession," he said. He said the exception was the economic downturn of 1991, which was prompted by the Gulf War.
"It is still true that the yield curve is a measure of incentives that banks have to lend -- whether it is business or consumer loans," Wieting said. "These relationships do not change much."
Smith said that before The Conference Board added the yield curve spread to the LEI, it was tested heavily.
"Only time will tell if it will work," he said. "The last recession ended in 1991, so it has been quite a period of time."

Lou Crandall, chief economist at R.H. Wrightson & Associates, suggested that the changes to the index are for naught. He said that historically, the slope of the yield curve was a very good indicator, in that a steep yield curve implied stronger economic activity, and the yield curve now works in the opposite way as prior years.
"The relationship held up through the early 1990s," Crandall said. "Then it became the darling of academic (economic) literature and inevitably ... it inverted."

One problem with leading indicators, he said, "is looking at what has worked with the hopes it will continue to work in the future," he added. "But as the structure of the economy changes, old indicators break down and composite indicators fail to work."
The spread between funds and the 10-year note currently stands at a relatively wide 110 basis points.

That indicates the Treasury market "is not looking at an immediate recession," said Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. But Platt is not convinced the yield curve can predict future economic activity.

"I cannot imagine that it has the longest lead of other indicators," he said. "I do not think the market wakes up, the curve flattens and that (implies) a recession. So, it is not a very, very early indicator. I tend to think of it as moderately contemporaneous."
Wieting suggested that another good leading indicator would be banks' willingness to lend money.

"Availibilty of credit is a leading indicator of consumer durable expenditures, which is a big component on the economy," he said. "An upward sloping yield curve encourages banks to lend ... Interest rates can be relatively low, but if banks are unwilling to lend then that can be a problem for consumer durables."
The Conference Board is scheduled to release the leading indicators index for November on Monday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867
